title: Follow the Cash: What September and October Revealed About Broadcom's AI Growth
subtitle: Strong results, new production capacity, customer financing and a new security offering: what each one means for cash that lasts.
summary: Behind every impressive set of financial results lies a more important question: how much of that growth can a company sustain? For Broadcom, the answer may depend on more than the strength of demand for AI chips.
content:
Behind every impressive set of financial results lies a more important question: how much of that growth can a company sustain? For Broadcom, the answer may depend on more than the strength of demand for AI chips. The AI boom has created an enormous opportunity for companies supplying the infrastructure behind it. The harder question, however, is whether that demand can be turned into cash that lasts.

In my last post, I looked at Broadcom’s two businesses: semiconductors and infrastructure software. This time, I want to follow the developments that have shaped the investment case from September into October 2026. The headlines point in different directions: strong results, new production capacity, customer financing, concerns about funding and a new software security offering. Taken together, they tell us why revenue growth is only the beginning of the analysis.

Strong growth needs a cash flow test

Broadcom’s fiscal third-quarter results, announced on 2 September, offered a striking picture of its AI momentum. Revenue reached US$29.591 billion, including US$16.7 billion from AI semiconductors. Operating cash flow was US$14.197 billion, and capital expenditure was US$532 million, leaving company-defined free cash flow of US$13.665 billion. Management also guided to fourth-quarter revenue of approximately US$34.8 billion, including US$21.7 billion from AI semiconductors (Broadcom, 2026b).

On my calculations, AI semiconductors accounted for about 56.4% of quarterly revenue, while free cash flow represented 46.2% of sales. These figures help explain why investors are excited: Broadcom is not merely talking about AI demand; it is already generating substantial revenue and cash from it. Yet the same numbers reveal a growing dependency. The more the investment case relies on AI, the more important it becomes to understand whether that demand can continue.

There is also a distinction between free cash flow and cash that can safely be distributed to shareholders. Acquisitions, debt repayments, customer financing and other commitments may compete for the same funds. Guidance is a forecast rather than a completed sale, too. If investors have already priced in exceptional growth, even a strong quarter may not be enough to meet expectations. I would therefore look beyond adjusted earnings and track whether revenue continues to turn into operating cash, and whether that cash remains available after the company’s other obligations.

Can Broadcom deliver what customers want?

Demand is only valuable if a company can fulfil it. On 29 September, Advanced Substrate Technologies, a joint venture between TOPPAN and Broadcom, opened a Singapore facility for advanced chip substrates. These substrates are used to package complex chips, and Broadcom’s announcement identified their availability as a supply constraint (Broadcom, 2026a).

The development connects the AI story to a more practical question: can Broadcom get the right components in place and deliver products on time? Additional substrate capacity could reduce the risk that shortages delay shipments and cash collection. It also brings the story closer to home, showing how a manufacturing investment in Singapore can affect a global technology company.

Still, opening a facility does not automatically mean it is operating at full capacity or earning an attractive return. From a capital-budgeting perspective, the future cash benefits must justify the investment and ongoing costs. Strong demand may allow fixed costs to be spread across more output; weaker demand could leave those costs weighing on returns. I would watch for evidence of production ramp-up, manufacturing yields and actual shipments. The question is not simply whether orders are growing, but whether Broadcom can turn them into profitable deliverables.

When the supplier also finances the customer

A report published on 1 October raised another consideration. Reuters reported that Broadcom had agreed to lend Anthropic up to US$42 billion to finance infrastructure spending, citing Anthropic’s IPO prospectus. The report said Broadcom could designate a financing partner and that the instruments could convert into Anthropic shares (Wang et al., 2026). The headline amount is a financing ceiling; it should not be read as proof that the entire sum has already been advanced.

There is a commercial logic to supplier financing. It can help a customer obtain equipment sooner, strengthen a long-term relationship and potentially generate a financing return. But it also means Broadcom must consider more than whether the customer wants its products. It must consider whether the customer can pay.

My concern is that sales risk and credit risk may move together. If an AI customer struggles to earn a return on its own infrastructure, it could reduce future equipment purchases while also finding it harder to meet existing obligations. Broadcom could then face slower operating cash flows at the same time as greater financing risk. A provision allowing a loan to convert into equity changes the form of exposure, but it does not guarantee recovery if the customer’s value falls.

Capital committed to financing customers is also capital that cannot be used for research, acquisitions, debt reduction or shareholder distributions. The right question is whether the expected return, after funding costs and possible losses, compensates Broadcom for that opportunity cost. I would want to distinguish the amount that could be lent from the amount actually drawn, identify who ultimately provides the funding, and examine collateral, maturity and guarantees. I would also avoid adding together separate financing headlines until it is clear whether the arrangements overlap.

The next constraint may be capital

On 12 October, Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan identified capital as a major constraint on AI expansion at a Singapore panel, while discussing progress in overcoming wafer and memory shortages. Reuters published its updated account on 13 October (Reuters, 2026). His comments link the production and financing stories: even if the hardware becomes available, customers still need the money to deploy it.

The financial mechanism is familiar. A project is worthwhile when the present value of its expected future cash inflows justifies the upfront investment. Higher interest rates or wider credit spreads increase financing costs and the return investors demand. Projects that once looked attractive may be delayed, even if the technology remains useful. For Broadcom, that could mean slower customer spending, delayed shipments or later cash collection.

Consider a simple illustration. A US$1 billion cash inflow expected five years from now is worth about US$620.9 million today when discounted at 10% a year. At a 12% discount rate, it is worth about US$567.4 million (8.6% less). If the payment arrives in year six rather than year five, its value at a 10% discount rate falls to about US$564.5 million. These are illustrative figures, not estimates of Broadcom’s cost of capital or fair value, but they show why the timing and funding of AI investment matter.

I would consider three possible paths. If funding remains available and customers use new capacity productively, Broadcom’s deliveries and cash collection could support continued investment. If financing becomes more expensive, customers may slow spending and supplier support may become less attractive. And if customers fail to monetise their AI services, demand and their ability to repay financing could weaken at the same time. These are scenarios rather than predictions, but they provide a useful framework for judging new information.

Software offers a different source of value

There is another side to Broadcom beyond AI chips. On 13 October, the company introduced VMware HyperArmor, a security offering for VMware Cloud Foundation environments (Broadcom, 2026c). Infrastructure software may generate revenue through purchasing decisions that differ from those driving custom AI chips, making it a potentially useful counterweight within the business.

A stronger security offering could help retain customers and make the existing platform more valuable. That is a reasonable hypothesis, not yet a proven earnings benefit: the announcement does not quantify additional revenue, and customers will still weigh alternatives, migration costs and subscription prices.

Infrastructure software accounted for approximately 30% of Broadcom’s third-quarter revenue, down from about 43% a year earlier, despite growing in absolute terms (Broadcom, 2026b). In other words, software can diversify the business while becoming a smaller part of the overall picture as semiconductors expand. I would look for evidence in segment cash generation and renewal trends before concluding that software fully offsets AI-related risk. A broad pullback in technology spending could affect both businesses.

What I would watch next

These developments shift my focus from the sheer size of the AI opportunity to the conditions required to realise it. Broadcom’s reported cash generation supports a constructive view of the business, but the outlook for shareholders depends on more than sales growth. Production must scale, customers must be able to fund their deployments, and financing risks must remain proportionate to the returns on offer.

My monitoring list is straightforward: whether revenue converts into cash; whether the new substrate capacity translates into reliable production and shipments; how much customer financing is actually drawn, guaranteed or otherwise exposed; and whether software growth and renewals continue to support the group. I would also compare AVGO’s share-price performance with broad-market and semiconductor benchmarks around major announcements. Relative performance can provide context, although it cannot prove that a particular announcement caused a price move.

I would become more confident if growing shipments came with timely cash collection and limited additional financing exposure. Rising sales alongside weaker cash conversion or expanding guarantees would make me more cautious. That is the question I keep returning to at The Financial Autopsy: does each new dollar of growth bring enough durable cash to compensate for the capital and risk required to produce it?
